title: How Do Gliders Fly? (3D, studio)
status: DRAFT: not voiced, not reviewed by a native speaker. Same facts and same shot order as script.json.

segments.text: A glider once flew more than three thousand kilometres in a single flight.
Yet a glider has no engine and no fuel. So how does it stay up?
Put your hand out of a moving car's window. Tilt your palm up a little: the air lifts your hand.
A wing does the same job. It turns the air downward, and the air pushes the wing up.
Its speed comes from height: like a sled on a gentle slope, it is always sinking slightly.
But only slightly. For every kilometre it sinks, it travels forty to fifty kilometres forward. An airliner with its engines out cannot reach even half of that.
And when the height runs out? A glider's real engine is the sky.
The sun heats the ground. Warm air rises like a column: a thermal.
The pilot circles inside that column and climbs as if riding a lift.
If the needle points up, the glider is gaining free height.
Wind that hits a slope turns upward too. The glider soars in that flow along the ridge.
And giant waves of air behind mountains have carried gliders above twenty-two kilometres. About twice as high as airliners fly.
Why are the wings so long and thin? Because the vortex at the wingtip slows the glider down. Longer, thinner wings make that loss smaller.
One condition: if you find no rising air, you land. So the pilot always keeps a landing field within reach.
No engine. No fuel. Just the sun, the wind, and a pilot who can read them.
